lines: Avery Brooks
+1 (555) 010-3319 | avery.brooks@example.com | example.com/in/abrooks
Date of birth: 9 Jan 1998 | Nationality: Brazilian
EDUCATION
Eastmoor University | B.S. in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Riverside Cinema | Box Office Attendant | Metro City, USA | Aug 2025 - Present
- Sold tickets and concessions during evening shifts and balanced the cash drawer at close.
- Trained 3 new attendants on the ticketing system and the refund policy.
Brightcart Retail | Data Analyst | Metro City, USA | Aug 2022 - Jun 2025
- Built the weekly retention dashboard for 2.4M customers that marketing used to retarget lapsed buyers, lifting 90-day repeat purchase from 22% to 27%.
- Cut the monthly revenue report from 3 days of spreadsheet work to 2 hours by moving it to scheduled SQL queries and a shared dashboard.
- Found customers with no orders by left-joining the orders table to the customers table and counting rows with a null customer name.

- Joining 40 source tables, deduplicating customer records across two loyalty systems and rebuilding the attribution logic in dbt-style SQL models, raised the share of orders tied to a campaign from 58% to 81%.
- Presented the quarterly customer review to the leadership team, and two of its three recommendations were funded in the next budget.
- Trained 20 merchandisers to answer their own questions with the self-serve dashboards, halving ad hoc data requests.
Pinecrest Insurance | Junior Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2020 - Jul 2022
- Ran the checkout A/B test until significance by checking the p-value every day and stopping on the first day it fell below 0.05.
- Analyzed 18 months of call-center data; my findings moved two agents to the evening peak and cut average hold time from 9 to 5 minutes.
- Writes the team's SQL style guide and review checklist, which cut query errors found in review by half.

- Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract while also maintaining the team calendar, answering ad hoc questions from sales, updating onboarding documents and covering the help desk on Fridays, which saved the fraud team 10 hours a month.
PROJECTS
City Bike-Share Demand Study | Independent Project | Python, SQL | Jan 2025 - Present
- Modeled hourly bike-share demand for 120 stations from 2 years of public trip data, forecasting next-day demand within 12% mean absolute error.
- Cut empty-station hours from 300 to 200 a week, a 50% reduction, in a replay of last summer's rebalancing.
- Raised forecast hit rate by 15% across 120 stations, from 60% to 75%, by adding weather and event features.
Food Pantry Visit Analysis | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Excel, SQL | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day, so the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut the Saturday line from 50 to 20 minutes.
- Cleaned 9,000 handwritten visit logs into a single table and matched repeat visitors, giving the pantry its first count of unique households.
- Wrote a one-page guide the pantry coordinator used to update the visit table each month after the project ended.
SKILLS
Tools: SQL, Python, Excel
Methods: dashboards, forecasting, metric design, data-quality checks

items.says: Date of birth and nationality should not appear on the résumé.
items.because: They are unrelated to qualifications, may invite inappropriate consideration, and use space.

items.says: The move from Data Analyst to Box Office Attendant is unexplained.
items.because: The current role may make readers question whether the candidate is still pursuing analytics.

items.says: Education appears before the more relevant Experience and Projects sections.
items.because: After five years of work, the analyst record is stronger evidence than the degree chronology.

items.says: “Sold” and “balanced” use past tense for a current role.
items.because: The verbs conflict with the entry’s “Present” end date.

items.says: The cash-handling line gives no transaction volume or balancing accuracy.
“Trained” uses past tense for a current role.
items.because: It conflicts with the entry’s “Present” end date.

items.says: The training line gives no result.
The Box Office Attendant entry gives an unrelated current role too much space.
items.because: Two bullets make it compete with more relevant analytics experience.

items.says: The dashboard line does not identify the analytical method or tools used.
items.because: A hiring manager cannot assess the hands-on technical work behind the outcome.

items.says: “That marketing used” can appear to modify the customers rather than the dashboard.
items.because: The ambiguity obscures who used the dashboard.

items.says: The join direction and null check are wrong for finding customers with no orders.
items.because: An orders-to-customers left join preserves orders, and a null customer name indicates an unmatched order.

items.says: The finding has no stated size, use, or business consequence.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether it identified a material population or led to action.

items.says: The increase from 58% to 81% is buried behind a long implementation sequence.
items.because: A scanning reader may miss the line’s strongest evidence of value.

items.says: “dbt-style SQL models” does not establish whether dbt was actually used.
items.because: A hiring manager cannot tell whether to credit direct dbt experience.

items.says: The customer-review line does not describe the analysis behind the recommendations.
items.because: The reader cannot connect the funded recommendations to the candidate’s evidence rather than presentation skill alone.

items.says: “To answer their own questions with the self-serve dashboards” is unnecessarily wordy.
Daily p-value checks and stopping at the first value below 0.05 do not establish valid statistical significance.
items.because: Repeated testing with optional stopping inflates the false-positive rate.

items.says: The A/B-test line gives no winning variant, effect against control, or resulting decision.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether checkout performance improved or the experiment informed an action.

items.says: “Until significance” omits “statistical.”
“By checking the p-value every day” is wordier than necessary.
The strongest Pinecrest result is not the opening bullet.
items.because: The hold-time reduction would establish analytical impact before the less conclusive experiment.

items.says: The call-center line does not show how the analysis justified moving two agents.
“My findings” uses a first-person pronoun inconsistent with résumé style.
“Writes” claims an ongoing responsibility in a role that ended in July 2022.
items.because: The present-tense verb conflicts with the employment dates and past-tense impact.

items.says: The reduction in query errors gives no underlying count or rate.
The unrelated administrative duties fragment the analyst narrative.
items.because: They distract from the fraud automation and make the entry look like a mixed task list.

items.says: The 10-hour saving is too far from the automation that produced it.
items.because: After the duty list, “which” can appear to refer to all the responsibilities.

items.says: The fraud-flag line does not identify the automation tool or process.
“12% mean absolute error” misstates the metric.
items.because: Ordinary MAE retains the target’s units; a percentage requires a normalized or percentage-based metric.

items.says: The demand-model line does not identify the model or validation approach.
items.because: The reader cannot assess the modeling choices or whether evaluation respected time order.

items.says: The error result gives neither its normalization nor a baseline comparison.
items.because: The reader cannot interpret what the percentage measures or whether the result is strong.

items.says: “Forecasting next-day demand” does not identify the intended operational decision.
“Within 12% mean absolute error” lacks an article in its current construction.
items.because: As written, the phrase is grammatically incomplete.

items.says: A drop from 300 to 200 is a 33% reduction, not 50%.
items.because: The decrease of 100 is 33.3% of the 300 baseline.

items.says: The strongest bike-share result is not the opening bullet.
items.because: The empty-station reduction would establish practical impact before the model description.

items.says: “A replay of last summer’s rebalancing” identifies neither the proposed approach nor the baseline.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what produced the improvement or how the comparison was constructed.

items.says: “Empty-station hours” does not say whether the figure is aggregated station-hours across the network.
The rise from 60% to 75% is 15 percentage points, not 15%.
items.because: Relative to the original 60% rate, the increase is 25%.

items.says: “Forecast hit rate” does not define what qualifies as a hit.
items.because: Without a success threshold, the metric cannot be evaluated.

items.says: “Adding weather and event features” gives no specific feature-engineering decision.
“Mapped” does not show how Excel or SQL was used to analyze the visits.
Matching repeat visitors does not by itself support a count of unique households.
items.because: Several visitors can belong to one household, so a household count needs household-level linkage.

items.says: The line does not state the resulting unique-household count.
“Matched repeat visitors” does not identify the record-linkage rule or fields.
“Cleaned 9,000 handwritten visit logs into a single table” illogically suggests physical logs were cleaned into a table.
“Each month after the project ended” gives a cadence but not the duration of continued use.
